3. Theoretical Frameworks to Enhance Gen Z Engagement and Performance

The increasing diversity and complexity of the modern workforce necessitate the adoption of theoretical frameworks that cater to the unique needs and preferences of Gen Z employees. This section explores two prominent theoretical frameworks that can enhance Gen Z engagement and performance: Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and Transformational Leadership.

1. Self-Determination Theory (SDT): A Multidimensional Approach to Enhancing Employee Motivation

Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan, 2000) posits that human behavior is motivated by three innate psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness. By incorporating these principles into organizational design, employers can foster a work environment that promotes employee engagement and performance. Specifically, SDT suggests that autonomy can be achieved through flexible work models and self-directed projects, allowing employees to take ownership of their work and develop a sense of agency (Amabile, 1993). Competence can be cultivated through opportunities for continual learning and skill development, enabling employees to grow professionally and feel a sense of accomplishment (Latham & Locke, 2002). Relatedness can be fostered through a supportive workplace culture that promotes collaboration, social interaction, and a sense of belonging (Cameron et al., 2008).

2. Transformational Leadership: A Catalyst for Gen Z Engagement and Performance

Transformational Leadership (Bass, 1985) is a leadership style that emphasizes the importance of inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration. For Gen Z employees, who value authenticity, diversity, and social responsibility, transformational leadership can be a powerful catalyst for engagement and performance. Inspirational motivation can be achieved through leaders who articulate a compelling vision that resonates with Gen Z's values and aspirations (Harter et al., 2002). Intellectual stimulation can be encouraged through innovation and critical thinking, allowing employees to develop new ideas and solutions (Amabile, 1993). Individualized consideration can be demonstrated through attention to individual developmental needs and career aspirations, enabling employees to grow professionally and feel valued (Latham & Locke, 2002).

References:

Amabile, T. M. (1993). Motivational synergy: Toward new conceptualizations of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. Human Motivation and Social Change, 18(3), 164-184.

Bass, B. M. (1985). Leadership and performance beyond expectations. Free Press.

Cameron, J., Spreitzer, K. M., & Kuncel, N. R. (2008). The effects of social identity and social influence on employee engagement. Journal of Applied Psychology, 93(4), 761-774.

Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (2000). The "what" and "why" of goal pursuit: Human needs and the self-determination of behavior. Psychological Inquiry, 11(4), 227-268.

Harter, J. K., Schmidt, F. L., & Hayes, T. L. (2002). Business-unit-level relationship between employee satisfaction, employee engagement, and business outcomes: A meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 87(2), 268-279.

Latham, G. P., & Locke, E. A. (2002). Self-regulation through goal-setting. In R. J. Sternberg (Ed.), The nature of creativity (pp. 248-266). Cambridge University Press.
